[RAZI-FULL:v29p104#2/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | reports | A second reading, close to 6:164, is that no sinful human or jinn is asked about their own sin; this raises a grammatical objection about the pronoun and the two agents. | mentions 6:164
[RAZI-FULL:v29p104#2/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | reports | To resolve the pronoun objection, one can treat “his sin” as an explicit noun phrase meaning a sinner’s sin, without a referential pronoun.
[RAZI-FULL:v29p104#2/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | prefers | The subtler, stronger grammatical solution places the pronoun’s antecedent before the verb: a sinner is not asked about his sin, whether human or jinn.
[RAZI-FULL:v29p104#2/r5] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | reports | The initial “then” may mark temporal succession after the sky splits, immediate logical succession as punishment starts without time for questioning, or rhetorical order after the failed attempt to escape through the heavens.
[RAZI-FULL:v29p104#2/r6] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | On the rhetorical-order reading, the warning first denies escape through the heavens, then says offenders will not even be given time to answer questions.
[RAZI-FULL:v29p104#3/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | reports | “Not asked” may mean no inquiry to identify the guilty, no rebuke asking why a sinner acted, or no request for pardon and intercession on another’s behalf.
[RAZI-FULL:v29p104#3/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | rejects | The intercession reading is challenged because “ask about” normally marks inquiry or reproach, while asking someone to grant something takes a direct object.
[RAZI-FULL:v29p104#3/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | In reply, a verb of asking can take two objects; with inquiry the second is omitted and the following prepositional phrase states what information was requested.
[RAZI-FULL:v29p104#3/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The intercession reading can construe each human as not asking about another human’s sin; the pronoun is attached to the grammatical subject as in “they killed themselves,” though it does not mean each killed himself.
[RAZI-FULL:v29p104#3/r5] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | On that construal, no human or jinn is asked to pardon another; all petition God, and God alone is the one asked at that time.
[RAZI-FULL:v29p104#3/r6] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | reports | An objection to the intercession reading is that the next verse’s statement that criminals are recognized by their marks does not fit it; al-Rāzī has supplied the grammatical and interpretive reply above.
[RAZI-FULL:v29p104#3/r7] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | reports | The apparent conflict with 15:92 and 37:24 has two answers on the common reading: the afterlife has different stations, or the sinners are questioned reproachfully rather than for information; the latter is better. | mentions 15:92, 37:24
[RAZI-FULL:v29p104#3/r8] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | prefers | The stronger reconciliation says they are not asked to identify what they did, but are asked why the agent did it, as a rebuke; under the second interpretation there is no conflict to resolve. | mentions 15:92, 37:24
[RAZI-FULL:v29p105/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | On the common reading, the lack of questioning humiliates the guilty, like descriptions of faces covered with dust and gloom or blackened on Judgment Day. | mentions 80:40, 80:41, 3:106

[RAZI-FULL:v29p105/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | On the intercession reading, the point is that no intercessor or merciful protector will be available to them.
[RAZI-FULL:v29p105/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Unlike worldly punishment, which God delays, afterlife punishment is not postponed even for the time needed to ask a question. | mentions 55:31

[BURHAN:v2p53/r1] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | holds | In analogy, claiming the same cause both to establish a ruling and to produce its opposite is contradictory; a distinction that adds to the cause reveals it was inadequately defined.

[BURHAN:v2p8/r1] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | holds | Prohibition can be inferred from explicit bans, threats, blame, expiation, phrases such as لا ينبغي, penalties, or descriptions of an act as corrupt or hated by God.

[BURHAN:v2p8/r6] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | holds | An act is legally sanctioned at least as obligatory or recommended when God or the Messenger praises, loves, approves, rewards, protects, forgives, announces security for, or swears by it or its agent.
[BURHAN:v3p256/r7] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | holds | Humans are often mentioned before jinn; the order may foreground the more astonishing creation, since jinn's creation is stranger. | mentions 55:39, 55:56, 72:5
